claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy.
The initial catalyst has baseline low-temperature activity, moderate poisoning resistance, and limited durability under transient engine conditions.
Nanoscale CeO2 islands will be deposited by physical vapor deposition.
The proposed deposition ranges from a sub-monolayer to a few nanometers of CeO2 at approximately 120 °C.
The deposited catalyst will receive a mild anneal at approximately 250 °C.
Optimized deposition will produce uniformly dispersed, well-adhered CeO2 islands.
CeO2 deposition will form finely dispersed, high-interface-area contacts between CeO2 islands and the alloy substrate.
CeO2-alloy interfaces will facilitate rapid oxygen exchange.
Dynamic CeO2-alloy interfaces will promote low-temperature oxidation reactions.
The CeO2-alloy interface will aid removal of poisoning species such as H2O and NO.
CeO2 islands will inhibit sintering and preserve the catalyst nanostructure during thermal cycling and extended use.
CeO2 deposition will reduce the light-off temperature to below 150 °C relative to the unmodified catalyst.
CeO2 deposition will improve resistance to H2O- and NO-induced deactivation during transient exhaust operation.
CeO2 deposition will improve long-term aging durability relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The unmodified catalyst has a higher light-off temperature and degrades rapidly under poisoning and thermal cycling.
The predicted improvements will persist under realistic transient low-temperature exhaust, H2O and NO exposure, thermal cycling, and mileage-related aging.
Nonuniform CeO2 island formation caused by variation in deposition parameters may alter catalytic performance.

contradictions.description: The anneal is described simultaneously as a vacuum anneal and as occurring in air; these are mutually incompatible atmospheric conditions unless a staged vacuum/air treatment is intended.
